subtitle: The short story: follow the object, and don’t name the feeling
words.intro: The German short story has a clear set of rules, and it grew out of the rubble of 1945. Begin abruptly. Name no feelings. Leave out the end. It’s the opposite of everything you’ve done in this book, and everything you’ve learned has made it possible.

grammar[0].fact: A short story written in German will often have a single object at the centre, and you don’t need to be told what it means. If you’ve followed the cup, you’ve understood the story. It’s also why the Abitur has been asking *Welche Funktion hat die Tasse?* since long before you were born.

grammar[1].fact: What’s left is C2.2: the voice you’ll have when you stop thinking about any of this. Few people who weren’t born here get as far as you have, and most who were born here don’t write as carefully. You can read a story with no ending, and know what it says.

document.intro: A real old postcard from a village, with four small pictures: a shop, a post office, a church and a forester’s house. It’s all there, and it says nothing. Somebody bought it, and somebody kept it. That’s a short story in itself.
document.fact: Postcards like this were sent in their millions around 1900. Guscht was then in the east of Germany, and today it’s in Poland.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Write a line about each picture, with no feelings.
reading.intro: Karl, Vienna and a certain Inge: in 1978 she lent him 300 marks. At a reading in Leipzig, Frau Huber gave Maya a sealed letter from Inge. This is what Maya wrote afterwards.
reading.fact: Wolfgang Borchert’s *Das Brot* is two pages long, about a couple and a slice of bread. Nobody says what it’s about. Many German schoolchildren have read it.
